new.title: Missing Light, Misleading Confidence: Optical-Module Readout Loss and Signal Reliability in Neutrino Telescopes
new.summary: Optical neutrino telescopes reduce the photomultiplier signals of an optical module or string segment to compact multichannel summaries, and readout loss can make these summaries unreliable. We asked whether availability-based quality gates, which accept a summary when enough of the readout was live, can certify a summary of inter-channel statistical consistency (called coherence here; not optical coherence) under readout loss, and where they fail. We used public IceCube pulses (9,484 string records) and the released hits of KM3NeT event KM3-230213A with controlled readout loss, together with a replay of real KM3NeT readout flags. In a two-by-two design we compared a published recursive support state with direct mask support, and calibrated every threshold on development records. The support state is a function of the mask and added no information. On IceCube the support-gated rule retained 0.16 percentage points more usable summaries, an effect of the window at which support was read that reversed sign at a looser tolerance; on KM3NeT it accepted nothing. The gates accepted only records with nearly intact masks, including records whose charge had been depleted by signal-dependent loss that the mask does not record. Pulse loss during live acquisition and timing jitter passed every availability gate, which then accepted summaries of which up to 66% were unreliable. Availability flags are therefore necessary but not sufficient, and signal-based checks are needed. This work uses public data and is not an IceCube or KM3NeT Collaboration result.

new.title: Analysis of Binary O-type Star Systems Using Recurrent Neural Networks
new.summary: This work presents an initial analysis of the estimation of effective temperature and surface gravity for simulated O-type binary systems using a recurrent neural network. The proposed system uses 34 equivalent-width measurements from the optical region of a stellar spectrum. Two methods were applied to observed IACOB spectra before normalization: the addition of a blackbody continuum and the addition of a second observed spectrum. The first method produces only small differences in the normalized line profiles and in the estimated physical parameters over 3700-7000~Å. In the second method, the secondary spectrum is added with contributions of 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, and 75 per cent, as defined relative to the original primary spectrum. The general comparison includes 192 simulated systems and 1152 modified spectra. For most of these spectra, the estimated effective temperature and surface gravity decrease as the contribution of the secondary component increases. Individual examples using HD14947, HD190429, HD48099, and HD206267 show that this behavior is not the same for every combination: some estimated effective temperatures fall below the estimates for both isolated spectra, and some surface gravity estimates increase. Comparisons with previously published values also depend on the physical parameter and reference considered. The results show that the proposed system is sensitive to the addition of a secondary spectrum, but do not establish a unique contribution for the secondary component of an observed binary.

new.title: Microbial Methanogenesis on Mars: A Life Detection Target for an MLE-Type Mission and Future Human Exploration
new.summary: Methane (CH4) is one of the most enigmatic and potentially consequential trace gases detected on Mars, having demonstrated apparent seasonality, localized plumes, or, depending on who you ask, never conclusively detected at all. While the Martian methane mystery remains unsolved, it has sparked a vibrant area of astrobiology research exploring whether microbial methanogenesis -- one of the simplest and most ancient metabolic pathways -- could plausibly proceed under various extreme physicochemical conditions characteristic of the Martian shallow subsurface. The emerging consensus is a cautious but compelling "possibly". These findings elevate methanogenesis as both a top priority candidate biosignature for extant life detection and a justification for urgently advancing in situ instrumentation capable of definitively detecting CH4 and constraining its origin, biotic or otherwise

new.title: rapidsim: A Python interface and cross-platform distribution framework for the RAPID protoplanetary disc simulation code
new.summary: The rapidsim is a Python package for the RAPID (Representative Approach for Particle-Integrated Disks) numerical simulation code, which is a modular one-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation code for modelling the evolution of protoplanetary discs and embedded dust particles written in C language. new.title: PRIMA prototype spaceflight KID readout electronics laboratory characterization
new.summary: We present further development and testing of prototype kinetic inductance detector (KID) readout electronics for the PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA). PRIMA is a NASA Probe-class astrophysics mission concept with two science instruments, FIRESS and PRIMAger, which provide spectroscopic and polarimetric imaging from 24 to 261 um. Together these instruments will explore the far-infrared sky with spatial-spectral mapping speeds that exceed previous studies by orders of magnitude, opening a vast discovery space. This increase in mapping speed is achieved by densely packed ultra-sensitive KIDs and cryogenically cooled optics. The PRIMA flight readout electronics will use the build-to-print SpaceCube Mini v3.0 which houses a radiation-tolerant Kintex KU060 field programmable gate array (FPGA). A custom high-speed digitizer board is being designed along with an RF electronics (RFE) board. The RFE was designed to provide programmable gain, band filtering, and RF switching between instruments. The prototype readout electronics, including the RFE, use functionally equivalent parts to the flight parts. In this proceeding we measure the readout loopback noise performance in the second Nyquist zone and timestream cross-talk performance. We present preliminary sweeps with the prototype readout coupled to prototype FIRESS detectors. Lastly, we demonstrate a cosmic ray pulse detection and real-time removal with an algorithm implemented in firmware.

new.title: Prospects for submillimeter VLBI of black hole photon rings with a stratospheric balloon-borne telescope
new.summary: Submillimeter very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) achieves higher angular resolution and probes more optically thin emission near supermassive black holes, with less interstellar scattering toward Sgr A$^*$. Above 345 GHz, however, the atmosphere confines ground-based VLBI to a few high, dry sites. Using 2012-2022 weather, we forecast what a 2.5 m telescope floating at 35-40 km, a successor to the 22 GHz Balloon-borne VLBI Experiment (BVEX) pathfinder, would add to ground-VLBI arrays at 345-690 GHz. The balloon adds little baseline length but reaches higher frequencies, where a fixed baseline is longer in wavelengths. On an ALMA-balloon baseline, Sgr A$^*$ at 460 GHz is at the detection threshold, with ten or more 20 s detections on about half of the simulated April days. These detections lie beyond the polarimetric photon ring transition, where the $n=1$ ring dominates the polarized visibility amplitudes. M87$^*$ at 460 GHz would need frequency phase transfer from a 230 GHz reference to be detected. With phase transfer, most Sgr A$^*$ detections beyond the transition at 460 GHz are on balloon baselines, whose thermal noise meets the linear-polarization threshold within one 300 s scan. At 690 GHz such detections require phase transfer that stays coherent at three times the reference frequency. In Fisher forecasts, a 460 GHz ring-geometry constraint requires balloons but is weaker than at 345 GHz, where balloons add little improvement. High-resolution 460 GHz VLBI science would require a 32 GHz bandwidth backend, submillimeter receivers, and simultaneous 230 GHz reference recording at every station.

new.title: Attitude Estimation of Falcon 9 Rocket Body Based on Photometric Characteristics
new.summary: The proliferation of space debris, driven by increasingly frequent space activities, poses a severe risk to operational satellites and future missions. Consequently, the surveillance and characterization of space objects have become critical. Current methods for attitude estimation of space objects often rely on target-specific models, such as those with a closed set of facets, and typically employ nonlinear filtering or machine learning techniques. However, these approaches often lack general applicability. This study proposes a more general approach to attitude estimation based on photometric light curves. We define a loss function that quantifies the discrepancy between the measured light curve and a theoretical model parameterized by the attitude parameters. By leveraging automatic differentiation to compute the gradients of this function, we use a gradient descent algorithm to achieve rapid and accurate attitude estimation. The proposed method provides a versatile and efficient framework for attitude estimation, overcoming the target-specificity limitations of existing techniques, with the parameters estimation time reduced to 15 seconds and the mean square error lowered to three decimal places. Validation on the third-party database demonstrates that the method exhibits strong generalization capability.

new.title: Inverse-designed tapers to improve throughput of on-chip astrophotonic spectrographs
new.summary: Astrophotonics offers a pathway towards compact and stable spectrographs for future large telescopes. The size of these spectrographs does not scale with the diameter of the telescope aperture; thus, they offer a cost-effective way to achieve astronomy science requirements compared to traditional optical spectrographs. A major limitation of current on-chip astrophotonic spectrographs is the significant loss incurred at interfaces between distinct components, particularly at the input and output fiber interfaces, limiting overall throughput. In this work, we investigate inverse-designed architectures to optimize transitions between these components to improve throughput. Inverse design formulates device design as an optimization problem, enabling non-intuitive geometries that can achieve high performance. We focus on optimizing coupling between an arrayed waveguide grating (AWG) spectrograph and an input single-mode fiber. Our approach explores two classes of fabrication-constrained inverse design. The first is shape optimization, which optimizes the geometry of the boundary of a coupling taper. The second is topology optimization, which optimizes the material distribution in a design region to gradually transform the optical mode between components. Both methods are implemented using the Tidy3D package from Flexcompute. We use germanium-doped silica for the core of the photonic components and silica as the cladding, and we use an SMF-28 fiber as input. This work demonstrates a pathway to improve astrophotonic spectrographs through computational inverse-design methods. Leveraging higher throughput, we can improve signal-to-noise ratios offered by photonic devices and position ourselves to design high-performance, cost-effective instrumentation for the next generation of telescopes, both on the ground and in space.

new.title: An Enhanced Intersecting-Lines Method for Optical Loss Characterization in SIS Heterodyne Receivers
new.summary: Accurate knowledge of radio-frequency (RF) losses in front of superconductor--insulator--superconductor (SIS) mixers is essential for optimizing millimeter- and terahertz heterodyne receivers. However, such losses are difficult to extract from conventional hot/cold-load measurements because the measured receiver noise combines contributions from the input optics, the mixer, and the intermediate-frequency chain. In this work, we present a numerical implementation of the straight-line, or intersecting-lines, method for estimating input-referred RF noise and optical loss from standard Y-factor measurements. Hot/cold IF spectra are acquired while sweeping the local oscillator (LO) pumping level from under-pumped to over-pumped operation, so that each IF frequency bin gives a family of linear relations between receiver output power and input load temperature. We evaluate all pairwise intersections between these lines and analyze the crossing cloud to obtain the effective RF input noise. We repeat the analysis across the IF band and multiple LO tunings which provides a frequency-resolved characterisation of the input losses over the full band. Our implementation turns the straight-line technique into a reproducible framework for receiver characterisation and relative optical-loss comparison in low-loss front-end configurations.

new.title: A 4-20 GHz Superconducting 90deg Hybrid Using Capacitively Loaded Coupled Lines for 2SB Heterodyne Receivers
new.summary: We report the design and cryogenic characterisation of a broadband superconducting 90deg intermediate-frequency (IF) hybrid covering 4 to 20 GHz for sideband-separating (2SB) heterodyne receivers. The hybrid is implemented in thin-film niobium using capacitively loaded edge coupled transmission lines, avoiding the air-bridge interconnections required in Lange-coupler layouts while retaining a compact superconducting implementation with low loss and good quadrature balance. Cryogenic measurements using Vector Network Analyser (VNA) show amplitude and phase imbalance better than 0.6 dB and 6deg, respectively, across the full band. When used in a 2SB receiver, this level of IF balance is consistent with the observed image-rejection performance in the 10-20 dB range, for the full receiver. The design supports the development of wide-instantaneous-bandwidth 2SB receivers for millimeter and submillimeter observatories, improving spectral grasp for broadband line surveys and high-redshift line searches.

new.title: MACE: Multigroup-Multiangle Integrated Thermal Compton Scattering Kernel
new.summary: We present a comprehensive set of accurate Compton-scattering tables for use in multigroup, multiangle radiation-transport calculations. The tables contain the exact thermal Compton kernel integrated over incident-energy groups, scattered-energy groups, and angular bins. To generate them, we develop a deterministic integration method in which the pointwise kernel is evaluated with a robust numerical treatment that remains accurate across challenging regions of parameter space. The multidimensional integrals are computed using nested quadratures whose panels adapt to the Compton recoil ridge, its thermal broadening, and the nearly elastic forward-scattering boundary layer. We validate the tabulated results against published kernel profiles, angular and energy moments, mean free paths, multigroup redistribution data, and an independent Monte Carlo estimator. The resulting tables provide the radiation-transport community with accurate, reproducible, and readily usable Compton redistribution matrices and angular moments.

new.title: Characterization of integrating-sphere systematic effects for photon calibration of the KAGRA gravitational wave detector
new.summary: Photon calibration (Pcal) systems are essential for accurately reconstructing gravitational-wave strain in laser interferometric detectors. In the KAGRA Pcal system, the laser power applied to the end test mass is measured using integrating-sphere power sensors. During the first part of the fourth observing run (O4a), repeated calibration measurements showed scatter larger than expected from the uncertainties assigned to individual measurements. Although this excess scatter was empirically reflected in the previously reported calibration uncertainties, its physical origin was not identified. In this study, we experimentally characterize the response of the integrating spheres used in the KAGRA calibration chain with respect to three incident-beam conditions: incidence angle, polarization, and beam position. Based on these measurements and the reproducibility of the integrating-sphere placement in each calibration configuration, we evaluate the corresponding systematic uncertainties and explicitly incorporate them into the uncertainty model for the O4a Pcal-X calibration measurements. The inclusion of these previously unmodeled effects substantially improves the consistency between the estimated uncertainties and the observed scatter, particularly for calibration parameters measured at the KAGRA end station, where the reduced chi-square values decrease from values as large as $10^3$ to values of order unity to several. These results indicate that variations in the incident-beam conditions of integrating-sphere power sensors account for a substantial part of the previously unexplained scatter and establish a more physically motivated framework for evaluating Pcal laser-power calibration uncertainty. They also provide a basis for future reduction of the calibration uncertainty through improved control of the incident-beam conditions.

new.title: Plate-YOLO: An End-to-End Object Detection Framework for Robust Astrometric Registration of Historical Plates
new.summary: Historical astronomical plates provide a long temporal baseline for time-domain astrophysics, but degradation and structural artifacts can hinder automated astrometric calibration. We present Plate-YOLO, a framework that combines source detection and stellar classification in one detector and supplies source catalogs to a separate astrometric solver. The detector adapts YOLOv5 with Space-to-Depth feature rearrangement, SimAM attention, a high-resolution P2 head, and a Normalized Wasserstein Distance loss for small bounding boxes. A Gaia-guided fine-tuning procedure uses initially solved plates to construct labels for a new archive. On 150 UBAI plates for which the conventional pipeline had failed, the Chinese-trained model solved 40 plates, and target-archive fine-tuning recovered a further 106, giving an overall recovery rate of 146/150 (97.3%). In the reported hardware configuration, source extraction took 6.61 s per plate for Plate-YOLO and 16.73 s for SExtractor. These results demonstrate the practical value of adapting source detection to degraded historical plates.

cross.title: Extending SOMPZ beyond Spectroscopic Coverage for Roman Weak Lensing
cross.summary: Precision weak lensing cosmology requires accurate galaxy redshift distributions. However, the spectroscopic samples used to characterize these distributions do not fully span the magnitude--color--redshift space of weak lensing source galaxies, necessitating extrapolation. This challenge will be critical at the depth of the Roman Space Telescope's High Latitude Imaging Survey (Roman HLIS). Using simulated LSST Year 4 and Roman HLIS photometry from the Cardinal simulations, we quantify how spectroscopic incompleteness biases photometric-redshift (photo-z) calibration and cosmological constraints. We find that the standard Self-Organizing Map p(z) (SOMPZ) method produces substantial tomographic bin overlaps and biased source redshift distributions. To address these limitations, we develop Roman-SOMPZ, which uses dedicated individual-galaxy photo-z estimators to supply redshift references for tomographic binning and redshift estimation. For the latter, we introduce UMAP-flow-z, an estimator that uses a UMAP embedding of deep-field galaxy colors to infer redshifts for phenotypes lacking spectroscopic representation. Compared with the standard pipeline, Roman-SOMPZ produces better-separated tomographic bins and lower absolute mean-redshift biases in eight of nine bins. Propagating the estimated redshift distributions into cosmological inference, we find that existing spectroscopy is adequate for early-stage weak lensing analyses in the Roman deep fields. Conversely, full medium-tier cosmology will require further improvements in redshift characterization.

cross.title: Radar and Infrasound Observations of the 2026 May 30 Cape Cod Bay Superbolide
cross.summary: Metre-scale impactors connect near-Earth-object dynamics, atmospheric-entry physics and meteorite delivery, but their pre-impact orbits and material properties are rarely measured together, especially for daylight events. We report observations of the 30 May 2026 Cape Cod Bay bolide. A very high frequency (VHF) meteor radar network detected atmospheric-entry plasma, weather radars detected falling meteorites, and infrasound sensors recorded the associated hypervelocity shock. VHF radar range--Doppler measurements resolve the meteor head echo from about 90 to 71 km altitude, while interferometric measurements localize short-lived non-specular plasma wake echoes down to an unusually low altitude of $\sim 30$ km. We identify this as the radar terminus, where breakup is expected to occur. A combined head-echo and trail fit constrains a steep southeastward trajectory over coastal Massachusetts. Weather-radar detections refine the dark-flight solution, place the likely fall region in Cape Cod Bay and constrain probable fragment sizes. Backward propagation of the fitted trajectory gives a heliocentric orbit near the cometary--asteroidal classification boundaries, with conflicting classifications from empirical dynamical criteria. Catalogue comparisons identify no convincing parent body or established meteor-shower association. Regional infrasound independently supports the terminal fragmentation region and yields an energy estimate of 0.5 kt TNT equivalent. The radar and dark-flight evidence are consistent with a dense, mechanically strong meteoroid, possibly iron-rich. The combination of meteor-radar plasma tracking, weather-radar observations of falling meteorites and infrasound measurements can provide accurate orbital elements and trace large meteoroids from atmospheric entry to nearly ground impact.

cross.title: Single-Transit Parameter Estimation with Calibrated Uncertainties
cross.summary: The growing volume of photometric data from current and upcoming exoplanet surveys demands automated analysis pipelines to detect and characterize exoplanet transit signals. Among these, single-transit events present a challenge, since only one event is observed, and standard transit-fitting techniques for periodic signals do not directly apply because they rely on phase-folding. Beyond detection, characterizing these events is equally critical for follow-up, yet existing approaches are either sensitive to stellar variability and require prior detrending, or depend on stellar priors and per-target fitting. This work presents a convolutional neural network that predicts transit depth, duration, and mid-transit time, together with calibrated uncertainties, directly from a single transit signal. Our network is trained on synthetic light curves and evaluated against a trapezoidal least-squares baseline. On 120 confirmed exoplanets, both methods achieve comparable median errors, but the baseline fails to locate the transit in 10% of cases, producing unreliable estimates that would propagate into follow-up prioritization. In contrast, our network fails in only 1% of cases, yields lower mean absolute errors, and does not require detrending or stellar priors. Detrending would distort or remove the transit along with high stellar variability, precisely where the baseline fails and our network succeeds. Finally, we identify 169 new transit candidates in TESS Sectors 27-60 and apply our approach to obtain their physical parameters, creating a catalog that includes single-transit, multi-transit and multi-planet systems. This approach offers a scalable path toward automated characterization of single transit events, a population that will grow with upcoming surveys.

cross.title: Spectroscopic Studies of Meteors within the Skytinel Network
cross.summary: We present 12 low-resolution meteor spectra recorded at four stations of the Skytinel network in Poland, focusing on consistent reduction and comparison of Fe, Mg, and Na emission features. Spectra spanning approximately 350--850 nm were extracted, background-subtracted, and wavelength-calibrated using IRAF. Corrections accounted for the wavelength-dependent quantum efficiencies of Sony IMX249 and IMX273 detectors and atmospheric attenuation as a function of observing geometry. The corrected spectra were decomposed into Fe, Mg, and Na components using selected atomic transitions, temperature-dependent emissivities, and pseudo-Voigt line profiles. Integrated Fe~I-15, Mg~I-2, and Na~I-1 intensities were compared in a ternary diagram. Most spectra overlap with or lie near the normal-meteor distribution in reference samples, while some extend toward Fe-rich or Na-rich regions. The most Fe-dominated event assigns approximately 81\% of the summed emission to Fe~I-15. These ratios characterize relative emission, not elemental abundances or bulk composition. Combined with trajectory and photometric data, spectral classification may help constrain plausible material properties in dark-flight models and refine predicted meteorite search areas.

cross.title: Multigroup Implicit Monte Carlo Radiation Hydrodynamics on Moving Voronoi Meshes with STORM and RICH
cross.summary: We present and validate an Implicit Monte Carlo (IMC) radiation-transport solver in the open-source, mesh-agnostic storm library, coupled to the moving-mesh hydrodynamics code rich in three-dimensional Voronoi tessellations. The solver is multigroup, or continuous in frequency, throughout; it transforms photon packets exactly between the comoving and laboratory frames, books every exchange with the material as a laboratory four-momentum so that the IMC path conserves energy to roundoff, formulates the Fleck factor in the fluid's proper time, and accelerates optically thick cells with multigroup Discrete Diffusion Monte Carlo (DDMC) behind an emissivity-preserving interface. We tested the solver on a broad suite of benchmark problems, and it performed well on all of them. The solver is built on the MPI-parallel Monte Carlo framework of storm, which scales to 13,440 cores.

cross.title: Reading Between the Lines: How Much Information Remains After Fitting a Stellar Spectrum?
cross.summary: What if we could model 100% of a stellar spectrum? Modern surveys infer stellar properties by comparing observed spectra with synthetic models, yet even the best fits leave structured residuals. We analyse 7087 GALAH survey spectra and ask what information remains after subtracting each best-fitting model. Across 13927 pixels, 4.5% of residuals exceed $3\sigma$, far above 0.3% expected from Gaussian noise. We map the amplitude, significance, sign, and recurrence of these residuals and identify 380 significant regions. Comparison with stellar atlases, line lists, diffuse interstellar bands, and sky diagnostics links most regions to plausible causes: 62% are candidate line-strength or line-profile mismatches, while others trace missing or unidentified lines, interstellar absorption, sky emission, or broader reduction structure. We then train data-driven models on the residual spectra themselves. Residual-only models recover $T_\mathrm{eff}$ to 80-150 K and [Fe/H] to 0.059-0.086 dex, depending on sample quality, and retain weaker, partly indirect information about elemental abundances. Extinction-related coefficients recover the strongest known interstellar features, whereas chromospheric activity leaves plausible Balmer-line signatures but is not recovered robustly out of sample. Most strikingly, the residual flux in 6% of wavelength pixels that were synthesised but excluded from the GALAH DR4 optimisation recovers stellar labels almost as well as the full residual spectrum and better than the remaining 94% alone. Residuals are therefore not merely imperfections to discard: they map missing line data, incomplete physics, unfitted astrophysical components, and observational systematics. Reading between the lines turns one spectroscopist's trash into another one's treasure, and provides a practical route towards extracting more of the information already present in stellar spectra.

cross.title: HyQ-LC: Improving Light-Curve Classification with Hybrid Quantum--Classical Learning
cross.summary: Light curves reveal stellar variability and support studies of stellar evolution and cosmic distances. Reliable classification is therefore important for large time-domain surveys. We present HyQ-LC for ten-class stellar light-curve classification using 359 handcrafted features and 633,034 training objects. The main model combines a window multilayer perceptron (MLP) backbone with a nine-qubit readout using amplitude encoding and angle re-uploading. Both this hybrid and its pure-MLP control have 44,238 parameters. On a shared 20,000-object test set, the hybrid has macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) point gains of 0.8276 and 1.2393 percentage points over the pure MLP on two fine-tuning seeds. A separate fixed-fusion configuration achieves slightly higher Macro-F1 but lower accuracy than approximately budget-matched LightGBM. Its positive class-level differences are concentrated in CEP, RRC, and ROT, while the full-budget LightGBM reference scores higher on both metrics. All circuits are simulated classically. The comparisons retain existing validation-selected checkpoints and use the same test objects, with features, predictions, and recomputation code publicly available. The results identify point-estimate improvements over the tested controls while leaving the specific contribution of the quantum branch unresolved.

cross.title: Searching for lensed gravitational waves with unlensed templates
cross.summary: Gravitational lensing can split the signal of a binary merger into two images, which either overlap and interfere or arrive as separate events. We show that the matched-filter output of every two-image template can be straightforwardly constructed from the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) time series that searches already compute with unlensed templates. This enables a marginalized detection statistic that increases search sensitivity without additional matched filtering and is more than 150 times faster than an explicit lensed template bank. For overlapping images in the geometric-optics regime, our two-image method recovers $\gtrsim97\%$ of the optimal SNR from point-mass and singular isothermal lenses, compared with as little as $67\%$ captured by unlensed templates, with substantial gains also for Chang-Refsdal and cored isothermal lenses. Overlapping lensed signals moreover fail the signal-consistency test that is used to down-rank noise transients. Our two-image method restores the consistency and increases the sensitive volume by roughly $2$-$4\times$ for the strongly down-ranked signals. For separated images, our method enables an efficient coherent search for pairs in which neither image is significant alone. Near fold caustics, this increases the sensitive volume by factors of 1.8-2.6 over requiring two independent detections, and up to 1.6 over a targeted counterpart search. Our method is applicable to any matched-filtering search.

cross.title: Linear Polarimetry of the Solar Corona during the Total Solar Eclipse of 8 April 2024: Multi-Band Observations and HDR Imaging
cross.summary: High-Dynamic-Range (HDR) multi-band linear polarimetry of the solar corona during total solar eclipses provides a vital ground-based diagnostic tool for mapping plasma morphology and magnetic topology in the inner and middle corona. Extracting reliable polarimetric signals requires rigorous observational calibration, spatial co-alignment, and noise reduction via stacking. We report optical linear polarimetric observations acquired during the 8 April 2024 total solar eclipse from Dallas, Texas, USA, near solar maximum. Using a full-frame color CMOS detector paired with an 80~mm refractor, multi-band Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) images were recorded simultaneously across three polarizer orientations ($-60^\circ$, $0^\circ$, and $+60^\circ$) using a 9-step exposure bracket ($1/800\text{~s}$ to $1/3\text{~s}$). We present an end-to-end data-reduction pipeline incorporating: (i)~a novel astrometric registration framework that reconstructs Sun-centric solar-disk coordinates via lunar-limb fitting, catalog star plate-solving, and ephemeris displacement calculations, achieving sub-pixel alignment; (ii)~a photometrically linear exposure-normalization HDR image synthesis; and (iii)~Multi-scale Gaussian Normalization (MGN) coupled with Polarization-to-RGB chromatic mapping. The resulting structurally enhanced polarization composites unravel a complex solar-maximum coronal topology characterized by helmet streamers and fine-scale striations traceable out to $\sim3\,R_\odot$. This framework establishes a high-resolution, photometrically calibrated dataset ready for subsequent polarized brightness ($pB$) and electron density inversions.

figures.caption: The figure shows the path of totality the April 8, 2024 total solar eclipse over the contiguous United States. The distinct line running directly through the middle of the purple/red band marks the centerline of the eclipse. Observers located exactly on this line experienced the maximum possible duration of darkness (totality). Stepping away from the central line reduces the the duration of the eclipse. cross.title: The EMA Justitia Probe: Terminator Frame-Based Deployment Orbit Selection and Surface Coverage Analysis
cross.summary: The Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt (EMA) probe is designed to perform asteroid imaging during an uncontrolled ballistic descent to (269) Justitia. The mission design is constrained by main spacecraft proximity operations, uncertain asteroid gravity, limited knowledge of the final deployment trajectory, and requirements for illumination and safe operations. These constraints necessitate a mission design that ensures suitable illumination, attitude determination and control, and payload pointing throughout descent. The EMA probe concept of operations employs near-terminator deployment orbit geometry with continuous Sun visibility and two attitude control modes: single-axis Sun-spin for periodic imaging opportunities and three-axis asteroid-pointing for continuous asteroid visibility. Based on these modes, formal requirements are derived for deployment orbits that enable asteroid observations during ballistic descent. A deployment orbit selection method is developed using the terminator reference frame and a minimum boresight deviation margin. The method identifies families of orbit orientations satisfying illumination and payload observation constraints. Reference orbits are selected and verified through mission geometry analysis and trajectory propagation using a polyhedron gravity model. Asteroid surface coverage is then evaluated for uncontrolled tumbling, Sun-spin, and asteroid-pointing modes. The results characterize the expected imaging performance and demonstrate the feasibility of the EMA probe concept for close-proximity asteroid imaging. The proposed approach can also support future ballistic probe missions subject to similar operational and observational constraints.

repl.title: Antenna Technology Readiness for the Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) Mission
repl.summary: The Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) will be the first sub-mm wavelength Space Very-Long-Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) mission. It targets astronomical imaging with the highest ever spatial resolution to enable detection of the predicted photon ring image feature of a supermassive black hole. BHEX is being proposed for launch in 2031 as a NASA Small Explorers mission. The BHEX science goals and the mission opportunity require a large, high precision, lightweight, spaceborne antenna. We present a survey of the technology landscape for realizing such an antenna. Technology readiness (TRL) for the antenna is discussed and assessed to be at TRL 5. A description of our technology maturation efforts towards TRL 6 is provided. Design studies leading to the preliminary design of a high efficiency antenna based on metallized carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) technology with a large 3.4 m primary reflector, a surface precision of < 40 {\mu}m to allow efficient operation up to 320 GHz, and a mass of only ~ 50 kg are outlined. Current plans anticipate attaining TRL 6 in 2027-28. Completed studies leading to the preliminary design point to a large margin in surface precision which also opens up applications at significantly higher THz frequencies, beyond BHEX.

repl.title: Redshift Assessment Infrastructure Layers (RAIL): Rubin-era photometric redshift stress-testing and at-scale production
repl.summary: Virtually all extragalactic use cases of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) require the use of galaxy redshift information, yet the vast majority of its sample of tens of billions of galaxies will lack high-fidelity spectroscopic measurements thereof, instead relying on photometric redshifts (photo-$z$) subject to systematic imprecision and inaccuracy best encapsulated by photo-$z$ probability density functions (PDFs). We present the version 1 release of Redshift Assessment Infrastructure Layers (RAIL), an open source Python library for at-scale probabilistic photo-$z$ estimation, initiated by the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC) with contributions from the LSST Interdisciplinary Network for Collaboration and Computing (LINCC) Frameworks team. RAIL's three subpackages provide modular tools for end-to-end stress-testing, including a forward modeling suite to generate realistically complex photometry, a unified API for estimating per-galaxy and ensemble redshift PDFs by an extensible set of algorithms, and built-in metrics of both photo-$z$ PDFs and point estimates. RAIL serves as a flexible toolkit enabling the derivation and optimization of photo-$z$ data products at scale for a variety of science goals and is not specific to LSST data. We thus describe to the extragalactic science community, including and beyond Rubin the design and functionality of the RAIL software library so that any researcher may have access to its wide array of photo-$z$ characterization and assessment tools.

repl.title: A targeted machine learning approach for detecting diffuse radio emission with Astronomaly: Protege
repl.summary: Diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters, such as radio halos, relics, and mini halos, is a key tracer of non-thermal processes, turbulence, and magnetic fields within the intra-cluster medium. However, their low surface brightness, as well as contamination from compact sources and imaging artefacts, makes their detection challenging. The sheer volume of data from instruments such as the Square Kilometre Array will render traditional manual-inspection based detection methods infeasible. This paper introduces a novel machine learning approach that uses active learning to rapidly identify diffuse emission candidates from a small, optimally-selected subset of data. We apply the self-supervised deep learning algorithm Bootstrap Your Own Latent to extract features from source cutouts in the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). We then pass these features through the Astronomaly: Protege anomaly detection framework to identify the final candidates. Using a human-labelled set, we evaluate our pipeline on high-resolution (~ 7''), convolved (15''), and combined-feature MGCLS datasets. Interestingly, the high-resolution features identify diffuse sources more efficiently than the convolved resolution, which are in turn outperformed by the combined features. Of the top 100 sources ranked by Protege, 98% exhibit diffuse characteristics, with 53% confirmed as cluster-related emission. Our work shows that Protege can identify diffuse emission with minimal human labelling effort, offering a powerful, scalable tool capable of detecting both known and novel diffuse radio sources.

repl.summary: he Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will repeatedly measure the brightness of billions of astrophysical sources using six colour filters. We test a simple idea: real physical signals tend to appear as coordinated patterns across several measurements, whereas noise does not; we call this behaviour ``coherence''. We illustrate the approach with three LSST-like simulations: (i) five Kuiper Belt Object (KBO) surface/activity states, (ii) 648 exoplanet spectra with an injected vegetation-red-edge-like spectral feature, and (iii) 500 multiband light curves. In idealised simulations, a weakly active KBO is strongly separated from its inactive counterpart when all five colours are combined. The injected red-edge-like feature becomes detectable at effective visible-disc coverage of about 13\%, and stacking about 150 detections could reach 5$\sigma$. Coherent, natural, and noise-like variability occupy distinct regions. A small Gaia DR3 stellar sample illustrates how colour and stability may help prioritise Galactic search regions.

repl.title: NAPTIME: A Neural-Process Framework for Rubin Alert Classification
repl.summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time will produce a high-volume stream of irregularly sampled multiband alerts for which spectroscopic confirmation will be available only for a small minority of sources. Tidal disruption events are rare phenomena that provide a direct probe of dormant massive black holes, but their light curves can be confused with nuclear variability and other transient subclasses. We present NAPTIME (Neural Astrophysical Photometric Transient Identification and Modeling Engine), a neural-process framework for photometric transient classification under sparse and partial observational context. NAPTIME models irregular multiband light curves directly, combining probabilistic light-curve reconstruction with classification and optional host-galaxy context, as well as photometric-redshift information. We evaluate on two simulated benchmarks: ELAsTiCC2, our primary Rubin-like broad-classification benchmark, and MALLORN, a photometry-only TDE-focused benchmark. On the 15-family ELAsTiCC2 task, the metadata-aware model reaches macro $\mathrm{F1} = 0.903$ and macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ($\mathrm{AUROC}$) $= 0.991$, while a matched photometry-only variant reaches 0.874 and 0.986. Viewed as a TDE-versus-rest ranking model, the classifier yields TDE average precision 0.985 with metadata and 0.979 without. Metadata is most valuable in the low-context regime. Using only the earliest 10\% of retained photometric measurements, macro F1 is $\sim$0.42 with metadata and $\sim$0.34 without it. On MALLORN, NAPTIME reaches macro $\mathrm{F1} = 0.693$ and macro $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.958$. These results show that neural processes provide a practical probabilistic framework for Rubin-like transient classification and remain effective for TDE-focused candidate recovery.

repl.title: STORM: RDMA-based Monte Carlo Transport Scheme for Distributed-Memory Particle Simulations
repl.summary: Monte Carlo particle transport enables high-fidelity astrophysical radiation and neutrino simulations - from core-collapse supernovae and neutron-star mergers to accretion flows - by handling multidimensional geometries, frequency dependence, and moving media without angular discretization. However, inter-rank communication limits scalability on unstructured meshes: standard two-sided MPI requires receivers to post receives and poll completions, creating per-iteration progress overhead that grows with the number of communication partners. Such problems have not demonstrated high scaling efficiency at $O(10^4)$ cores. We present STORM (Scalable Transport via One-sided Remote Memory), an open-source library for Monte Carlo transport on general meshes, physics, and boundary conditions. STORM provides a lock-free, mesh-independent communication layer that replaces MPI's matched-send/receive semantics with Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) - one-sided operations that write directly into a remote rank's memory without involving its CPU. Each rank pair shares a single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer; RDMA writes transfer particles while receivers remain passive. A two-sided MPI backend provides a portable fallback. In an adversarial uniform-emission benchmark, the RDMA backend sustains $>97\%$ weak-scaling and $>88\%$ strong-scaling efficiency up to 13,440~cores (112~cores per network adapter), with $1.14$-$1.27\times$ speedups over the two-sided alternative. In a Hohlraum IMC benchmark at 4480 ranks, it is $1.41\times$ faster because MPI progress overhead is reduced by $6.1\times$. By decoupling communication from physics models and mesh representations, STORM removes a barrier to scaling Monte Carlo transport in astrophysical multiphysics codes, enabling coupled radiation-hydrodynamics with energy- and angle-resolved photon or neutrino transport on dynamically evolving meshes at scale.

repl.title: Consistency and precision of very long baseline interferometry source coordinate time series
repl.summary: Coordinate time series of extragalactic radio sources from very long baseline interferometry observations are widely used to evaluate source positional stability, select stable sources for celestial reference frames, assess reference-frame axis stability, and investigate source-related astrometric variability. Their external consistency, realistic errors, and relation to processing strategies and analysis configurations remain to be investigated. We aim to compare coordinate time series solutions from different analysis centers and investigate how processing strategies and configurations contribute to their differences. We collected eight solutions from seven analysis centers and selected 496 common sources after data selection, reference-frame alignment, and extraction of common observing sessions. Inter-solution differences were characterized with pairwise positional offsets and correlation analysis, and realistic positional errors with the N-cornered-hat (NCH) method and bootstrap resampling. Most solutions have median weighted root mean square (WRMS) values of a few hundred microarcseconds $(\mathrm{\mu as})$, and the median NCH-derived precision is about 200-300 $\mathrm{\mu as}$ in right ascension and 250-400 $\mathrm{\mu as}$ in declination. Solutions with similar strategies, software, or source constraints show higher consistency, with more similar WRMS values, stronger correlations, and closer precision estimates. Consistency is affected not only by the global or independent mode distinction but also by detailed analysis configuration. NCH-derived precision depends on declination, being poorer in the southern sky, and stabilizes with more observing sessions. Processing strategies and configurations introduce marginal differences; solutions remain generally consistent. Inter-solution comparisons independently estimate realistic stochastic errors beyond formal errors.

repl.title: Error Propagation from Integral Moments and Spectral Derivatives of Stokes Profiles to Magnetic Observables
repl.summary: We aim to derive convenient analytic estimations of magnetic inference errors, which can be used to inform and facilitate the creation of the science-traceability matrix of a polarimetric instrument. In order to do this, we study the general problem of the propagation of Poissonian noise in polarized light signals to derived data products of the Stokes profiles, namely integral moments of arbitrary orders and spectral derivatives of the intensity. In particular, we derive the errors on the longitudinal and transversal projections of the magnetic field inferred from the weak-field approximation (WFA) of the Zeeman effect. The propagated errors on magnetic inference are traced back to the signal- to-noise ratio (SNR) of the observations. The results can be used to quantify the contributions of different environmental and instrumental conditions (spectral line width, spectral resolution, line spread function, stray light) to the overall error on the inferred quantities. Our tests indicate that the integral-moment method of inference is comparable to the local derivative in a predictable way.

repl.title: The dawn of the first galaxies
repl.summary: Understanding how the first galaxies assembled their stellar mass at cosmic dawn is a central frontier of modern astrophysics. JWST has now revealed an unexpected population of ultraviolet-bright galaxies at z>10, whose intense emission points towards a rapid stellar mass growth that challenges current models of early galaxy assembly. Yet, the cold gas fueling this growth remains hidden: current ALMA sensitivity restricts routine detection to only the brightest ionized-gas tracers such as [OIII] 88$\mu$m, while [CII] 158$\mu$m, a key coolant and gas-mass proxy of the neutral interstellar medium (ISM), is undetected beyond $z\sim8$. This leaves fundamental questions unanswered: how quickly primeval galaxies gathered cold gas and turned it into stars; what physical conditions (density, temperature, radiation field) characterized their ISM; how fast metals and dust built up; and how feedback regulated early gas assembly. Only a transformational sub-millimeter facility like ALMA2040 can address these questions, enabling systematic surveys of [CII] in the first galaxies and providing a representative census of gas fractions and depletion times. A simulated galaxy at $z=11.3$ shows that ALMA2040 not only will detect, but also spatially resolve its merging cold-gas structure in [CII] on $\sim$200 pc scales in 5 hours (below 100 pc in 10 hours). ALMA2040 will also spectrally resolve multiple lines simultaneously, akin to integral-field spectroscopy, providing the key diagnostics needed to break density-metallicity-radiation-field degeneracies and map the multi-phase ISM of z>10 galaxies. The combination of dramatically increased line sensitivity and wide instantaneous bandwidth will push the search for the first galaxies out to the earliest cosmic times, with [OIII] detectable up to $z\sim20$. ALMA2040 will thus be transformative for understanding how the first galaxies assembled at cosmic dawn.

repl.title: Relative Jump Distance: a diagnostic for Nested Sampling
repl.summary: Nested sampling is widely used in astrophysics and cosmology to reliably infer model parameters and compare models within a Bayesian framework. To address models with many parameters, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) random walks are used within nested sampling to advance a live point population. Diagnostics for nested sampling inference are essential to verify that trustworthy astrophysical conclusions can be drawn. We develop a diagnostic to identify poorly mixed random walks that do not meet the requirements of nested sampling. The distance from the start to the end of the random walk, the jump distance, is compared to the typical neighbour distance between live points, to obtain a relative jump distance (RJD). A robust estimate of a typical neighbour Mahalanobis distance is obtained with the MLFriends algorithm. In mock and real-world inference applications such as inferring the distance to GW170817, we observe the relative jump distance. We propose the geometric mean <RJD> and fraction of RJD>1 as new summary diagnostics. To evaluate the sensitivity of the new diagnostics, problematic runs are identified by comparison with reruns using much longer MCMC chains. Trustworthy inference runs are consistently associated with <RJD> above 1.1, while problematic runs can fall below these thresholds. The RJD is more sensitive than previous tests based on the live point insertion order. The RJD diagnostic is proposed as a widely applicable diagnostic to verify inference with nested sampling. It is implemented in the UltraNest package in version 4.1.

repl.title: Robustness of Neural Networks for CMB Polarization Foreground Removal
repl.summary: The detection of Cosmic Microwave Background primordial $B$-mode polarization would constitute a ``smoking gun" signal of primordial gravitational waves. However, this measurement requires accurate removal of polarized Galactic foregrounds to avoid systematic biases when estimating the tensor-to-scalar ratio. Methods based on Machine Learning techniques (ML), such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have recently been proposed as alternative foreground cleaning techniques, but their applicability to real data relies on their ability to generalize beyond the models assumed during training. In this work, we focus on a variety of foreground models (FMs) used for training and conduct a systematic study of the generalization properties of a CNN-based method. We train various CNN architectures on simulations generated from different Galactic FMs, and test their performance on models not used during the training. By characterizing the statistical properties of the FMs using variance, skewness, and Shannon entropy, we define a statistical complexity hierarchy among them. We show that training on the more complex FMs reduces bias and improves precision when testing on unseen FMs, whereas training on the simplest model could introduce systematic errors. These results evidence that a lack of generalization is a relevant source of systematic uncertainty, and emphasize the importance of understanding the impact of the models assumed during training in ML-based methods before applying them to real data.

repl.title: SPLIT: Loosely-coherent inference of long-inspiral gravitational-wave sources for robustness against modeling and data outliers
repl.summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves (GWs) from dozens of extreme- and intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs/IMRIs). These sources will stay in-band for months to years, offering extraordinary scientific potential. However, their fully phase-coherent analysis standard in current pipelines imposes stringent waveform accuracy requirements; failing to model the signal over such long durations can result in significant systematic biases. To address this, we formulate a robust Bayesian inference framework that segments the data into blocks, infers each block coherently, and recombines the results using loosely-coherent phase information. By restricting full phase-tracking to much shorter block durations, this approach prevents significant accumulation of phase errors. We implement this methodology in \textsc{SPLIT} (Segmented Posteriors for Long-Inspiral Templates), a GPU-accelerated Python package. Applying \textsc{SPLIT} to an environment-rich injection, we demonstrate that while a fully-coherent vacuum-GR analysis incurs a maximum 1D systematic bias of $\approx 4.8\sigma$ from the truth, the shorter integration window of our loosely-coherent approach restricts such biases to $\lesssim 0.5\sigma$. Overall, despite a fractional loss of optimal signal-to-noise ratio, the substantial improvement in parameter accuracy offered by our method presents a highly advantageous trade-off for LISA and other future GW detectors.

repl.title: A cross-calibration approach for polarisation-sensitive detectors in CMB experiments: application to LiteBIRD's polarisation angle calibration
repl.summary: We present a cross-calibration algorithm that determines the relative calibration of detectors within the same frequency band of a CMB experiment. The method iteratively compares single-detector maps with frequency-band maps, and it can be applied to any calibration parameter that can be corrected through reprocessing of the instrument's data at the map level. This allows for validation and correction of calibration both before and after observations. We validate the pipeline by calibrating the polarisation angle of simulated sky maps from the upcoming \textit{LiteBIRD} experiment. The cross-calibration algorithm has been tested both in the case of random miscalibration of each individual detector and in the case of rotation of entire detector wafers. In both cases, the cross-calibration algorithm converges to the correct value and we are able to identify and correct relative miscalibrations in the polarisation angle of each detector with arcminute precision. Absolute calibration can then be addressed either through ground-based measurements, or through the $E$-$B$ nulling technique. To assess compliance with \textit{LiteBIRD}'s systematics budget, we propagate the residual miscalibration uncertainties through component separation and tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$) estimation pipelines using both parametric (\texttt{FgBuster}) and blind (\texttt{HILC}) methods. In both cases, the induced bias on $r$ remains well below the \textit{LiteBIRD} maximum budget for systematics of $\delta r < 6.5\times10^{-6}$. This confirms that the cross-calibration method presented is suited for use in modern high-precision CMB experiments.

repl.title: When X-ray Features Fail to Identify Intrinsic Emitters: Label Noise and Luminosity Overlap in Machine Learning Classification of AGN and Star-forming Galaxies
repl.summary: Previously, we found that adding an X-ray flux feature to a Random Forest classifier of active galactic nuclei (AGN) and star-forming galaxies (SFGs) coincided with a decrease in classification accuracy from 97.51% to 89.26%, a counterintuitive result given the prevailing theory that X-rays are a reliable AGN diagnostic. We investigate this discrepancy through both astrophysical and machine learning lenses. On the astrophysical side, we show that the X-ray luminosities of AGN and SFGs in the sample substantially overlap across the canonical $10^{42}$ erg/s threshold, reflecting the moderate luminosity characteristic of an optically-selected sample and the contribution of high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) to SFG emission. On the machine learning side, we argue that BPT-derived training labels carry instance-dependent label noise concentrated near the BPT demarcation line, where X-ray data would be most useful as a discriminator. We show that objects misclassified in 5-fold cross-validation cluster near the Kewley demarcation curve, with a median distance of 0.123 dex versus 0.743 dex for correctly classified objects (Kolmogorov-Smirnov $D = 0.745,\; p = 1.67\times 10^{-9}$). A controlled cross-validation decomposition shows that the previously reported decrease reflects predominantly sample selection: on a fixed sample, adding the X-ray feature leaves class-resolved metrics unchanged, and its permutation importance is consistent with zero across resampled splits. The classifier therefore makes negligible use of a physically informative feature, consistent with training labels coupled to the optical features. We conclude that future classifiers operating on optically-selected samples should employ independent label sources or noise-robust training methods.

repl.title: A deep learning algorithm for black hole spin estimation using hot-spot secondary images
repl.summary: Sagittarius A* exhibits frequent flaring activity across the electromagnetic spectrum that is often associated with a localized region of strong emission known as a hot spot. We aim to train a deep learning model to provide a link between key parameters of this phenomenon - hot-spot emission radius, and black hole inclination and spin - to the observed angle difference between the primary and secondary image ($\Delta PA$) that present and future interferometric arrays could resolve. Using the general relativistic radiative transfer code IPOLE, we generated a library of $\sim100.000$ models with varying system parameters and computed the position angle difference on the image plane between the primary and secondary images of the hot spot. We explore equatorial and non-equatorial circular orbits and evaluate our models against approximate observational constraints, including partial-orbit visibility and observational errors. Our algorithm STIHOS shows remarkable accuracy in calculating spin and inclination from the majority of the observational tests we perform ($\sigma_{a_*}=0.04,\,\sigma_i=2^{\circ}$), even in extreme conditions where only half of the orbit is visible. The off-equatorial estimation provides softer constraints in the absence of prior information. Our results demonstrate the importance of hot-spot observations for spacetime estimations. Given the increasing efforts to detect the photon-ring, our framework could prove valuable in interpreting the first observations of lensed emission.

repl.title: Gravitational-wave parameter estimation with machine-learning generated surrogate waveforms
repl.summary: The worldwide network of gravitational-wave detectors have detected more than 350 binary coalescence events till date. Future third-generation detectors, like Einstein telescope, are expected to detect orders-of-magnitude more signals from sources with more complicated characteristics, including eccentric orbits and high-mass ratio binaries. It is well-established that the computational cost of parameter estimation for signals from these kinds of sources will be extremely high. In particular, the process could be sped-up if generating theoretical waveform predictions, used for likelihood calculation becomes faster. Recently, various machine-learning techniques has been proposed to this end. In this work, we propose a two-stage deterministic conditional-autoencoder model for generating four-parameter SEOBNRv4 waveforms. The first-stage of the model generates amplitude and phase series of the waveform, while the second-stage calibrates the residual error in the predictions. Our model achieves a median mismatch of around $10^{-2}$ with the target polarization waveforms, while the calibrated amplitude/phase series achieve $10^{-6}$ level cosine distance error. We then propose a waveform conditioning step to enable use of these surrogate waveforms for downstream parameter estimation tasks. Finally, we perform extensive parameter estimation tests, with ML and EOB waveform injections and try to recover posterior estimates for the source parameters. We find that when ML waveforms are used to recover EOB target parameter estimates, the inferred posterior have some systematic bias. This inherent bias can be estimated and corrected for, and then importance reweighting of posterior samples can enable use of low-accuracy surrogate waveforms at low SNRs.

repl.title: Calibration of the Next Generation Palomar Spectrograph as a Stellar Speedometer
repl.summary: We calibrate the Next Generation Palomar Spectrograph (NGPS) for precision stellar radial-velocity (RV) measurements using repeated observations of 24 Gaia-ESO RV standards spanning $G=11$-$18$. Because NGPS is mounted at the Hale telescope's Cassegrain focus, changes in instrumental flexure produce wavelength-solution shifts of tens of km s$^{-1}$, with substantial time and wavelength dependence. We develop a pipeline that measures these shifts directly from each science exposure, using telluric absorption features in the R and I channels and the [O I] 5577 Å sky-emission line in the G channel. This approach eliminates the need for frequent on-sky arc calibrations. The resulting wavelength-dependent flexure corrections reduce the median absolute discrepancy relative to Gaia-ESO RVs from tens of km s$^{-1}$ to 1.6 km s$^{-1}$. Telluric absorption provides substantially more reliable flexure calibration than sky emission lines, which do not track point-source illumination of the slit. The I channel, which contains both many telluric lines and strong photospheric lines across a range of spectral types, generally yields the most stable RVs. The achieved precision remains above the photon-noise limit, indicating that NGPS RV performance is currently limited by calibration and modeling systematics. These results demonstrate that NGPS is well-suited for accurate and precise stellar RV measurements across a wide range of astrophysical studies.

repl.title: MADGRAV: a multilevel anomaly-detection pipeline for gravitational-wave searches applied to LIGO data
repl.summary: We present the results of \textbf{MADGRAV}, a deep-learning-based search for high-mass compact binary coalescences, applied to the data collected by the LIGO interferometers during the third observing run and during the first and second part of the fourth observing run. The \textbf{MADGRAV} pipeline consists of a series of sequential convolutional neural networks that perform anomaly detection, glitch classification, coherence testing, and signal ranking. Data from the Hanford and Livingston LIGO detectors are studied (both individually and in coherence) by way of 1 second Q-transform windows. Of the candidates that survive every stage of the pipeline, 48 reach the significance threshold, and we report 47 gravitational wave detections characterised by a false alarm rate below $1\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ with a probability of astrophysical origin $p_{\rm astro}>0.9$. Of the 47 detections, 44 are shared with the minimally modelled coherent WaveBurst search. The observed total source-frame masses, extracted from official gravitational wave transient catalogues, are in the $14-236 M_{\odot}$ range with a median of $69 M_{\odot}$, and a median SNR of 16. We note that the recovered fraction of confident detections rises with mass: for LIGO detectors network SNR $>10$ the pipeline recovers $8.1\%$ of confident catalog events below $30 M_{\odot}$, $39.8\%$ between $30$ and $100 M_{\odot}$, and $53.3\%$ above $100 M_{\odot}$, corresponding to $33.3\%$, $45.5\%$ and $53.3\%$ of the events detected by coherent WaveBurst in the same bins. These results suggest that anomaly detection pipelines can serve as an independent detection channel complementary to matched filtering in the high-mass high-SNR regime.

repl.title: Dark Matter Particle Explorer: Ten-Year On-Orbit Performance and Scientific Outcomes
repl.summary: The Dark Matter Particle Explorer (DAMPE, also known as ``Wukong'') is the first scientific space mission within the framework of the Strategic Pioneer Program on Space Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The main scientific objectives of DAMPE include indirect detection of dark matter, cosmic-ray physics, and high energy gamma-ray astronomy. Thanks to its large geometrical factor and thick imaging calorimeter, DAMPE could effectively detect cosmic-ray electrons (including positrons) and gamma-rays up to 10~TeV, and nuclei up to PeV. Since launched on 17 December 2015 into a Sun-synchronous orbit, DAMPE has been smoothly operating on orbit for more than ten years. Here we present an overview of instrument, on-orbit status, and highlight scientific results of DAMPE, including the measurements of the all-electron energy spectrum and the spectra of protons and other nuclei, and high energy gamma-ray line search.
